questions.question_text:
y = 4x^3 - 7x^2 + 5x - 10
(a) Find in simplest form
(i) dy/dx
(ii) d^2y/dx^2
(3)
(b) Hence find the exact value of x when d^2y/dx^2 = 0
(2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) M1: differentiates, reducing the power of at least one term by 1, e.g. x^3 -> x^2, x^2 -> x, 5x -> 5, or -10 -> 0. A1: correct simplified derivative dy/dx = 12x^2 - 14x + 5 (indices must be fully processed). (ii) A1ft: correct simplified second derivative d^2y/dx^2 = 24x - 14, or follow through their first derivative differentiated again (must be simplified). (3 marks)
(b) M1: sets their second derivative of the form ax + b (a,b ≠ 0) equal to 0 and proceeds to a value for x (condone slips in rearranging as long as a value for x is obtained). A1: correct exact value x = 7/12 (allow exact equivalents such as 14/24 but not rounded decimals e.g. 0.583). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
Jamie takes out an interest-free loan of £8100. Jamie makes a payment every month to pay back the loan. Jamie repays £400 in month 1, £390 in month 2, £380 in month 3, and so on, so that the amounts repaid each month form an arithmetic sequence.
(a) Show that Jamie repays £290 in month 12
(1)
After Jamie's Nth payment, the loan is completely paid back.
(b) Show that N^2 - 81N + 1620 = 0
(2)
(c) Hence find the value of N.
(2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1*: correct working to obtain 290, e.g. (u12=) 400 + 11×(−10) = 290, or 400 − 110 = 290. Must be a correct calculation with brackets correctly placed (or recovered). (1 mark)
(b) M1: uses a correct sum formula for an arithmetic series in terms of N with a = 400 and d = −10 (or +10) and sets the sum equal to 8100, e.g. 8100 = (N/2)(2×400 + (N−1)×(−10)). A1*: fully correct proof with sufficient working shown (all brackets removed to give the unsimplified expanded quadratic) leading to the given answer N^2 − 81N + 1620 = 0, with no unrecovered errors. (2 marks)
(c) M1: solves the given quadratic equation by any correct method to obtain at least one value for N, e.g. (N−45)(N−36) = 0 => N = 45, 36. A1: realises the smaller value is required and selects N = 36, clearly rejecting N = 45 (e.g. by underlining or omitting it). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
The point P(3, –2) lies on the curve with equation y = f(x), x ∈ ℝ. Find the coordinates of the point to which P is mapped when the curve with equation y = f(x) is transformed to the curve with equation
(i) y = f(x – 2)
(ii) y = f(2x)
(iii) y = 3f(–x) + 5
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(i) B1: (5, −2), i.e. x = 5, y = −2 (translation +2 in the x-direction adds 2 to the x-coordinate of P). (1 mark)
(ii) B1: (1.5, −2), i.e. x = 1.5, y = −2 (horizontal stretch scale factor 1/2: the x-coordinate satisfying 2x = 3 is x = 1.5, y-coordinate unchanged). (1 mark)
(iii) B1: one correct coordinate, e.g. x = −3 (from −x = 3) or y = −1 (from 3×(−2)+5 = −1). B1: both coordinates correct, (−3, −1) (note B0B1 is not a valid mark profile — the x-coordinate must be correct to score the second mark). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
A sequence u1, u2, u3, ... is defined by
u_(n+1) = k*u_n - 5
u1 = 6
where k is a positive constant.
Given that u3 = –1
(a) show that
6k^2 - 5k - 4 = 0
(2)
(b) Hence
(i) find the value of k,
(ii) find the value of sum_(r=1)^(3) u_r
(3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: correct application of the given recurrence relation using u1 = 6 to find u2 = 6k − 5, and then u3 = k(6k−5) − 5 in terms of k, setting u3 = −1. A1*: obtains the printed answer 6k^2 − 5k − 4 = 0 with no errors, including the '= 0' (this is a given answer, so slips must be recovered before the final line). (2 marks)
(b)(i) B1: deduces the correct value k = 4/3 (ignore any working, just look for this value; must be clear that k = 4/3 is selected and not the other root k = −1/2, since k is given as positive). (ii) M1: attempts the second term using their k, e.g. (4/3)×6 − 5, and adds u1 = 6 and u3 = −1 to it, e.g. 6 + [(4/3)×6 − 5] − 1. A1: correct value of 8, with no other value offered unless rejected (correct answer with no working scores both marks). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Given that θ is small and in radians, use the small angle approximations to find an approximate numerical value of
(θ tan 2θ) / (1 - cos 3θ)
(3)
questions.mark_scheme_text: B1: uses tan 2θ ≈ 2θ or 1 − cos 3θ ≈ 1 − (1 − (3θ)^2/2) = (3θ)^2/2, or equivalent (may be seen when working on the numerator or denominator separately, or within the fraction). M1: attempts to use both correct small angle approximations together in the given expression, i.e. θ×(2θ) / [(3θ)^2/2] (condone poor bracketing, but do not allow an incomplete denominator such as 1 − (3θ)^2/2 written as just (3θ)^2/2 without the '1 −'). A1: correct value 4/9 (do not allow rounded decimals such as 0.444, but allow a clearly indicated recurring decimal, e.g. 0.4 recurring). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of the curves with equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) where
f(x) = e^(4x^2 - 1), x > 0
g(x) = 8 ln x, x > 0
(a) Find
(i) f'(x)
(ii) g'(x)
(2)
Given that f'(x) = g'(x) at x = α
(b) show that α satisfies the equation
4x^2 + 2 ln x - 1 = 0
(2)
The iterative formula
x_(n+1) = sqrt( (1 - 2 ln x_n) / 4 )
is used with x1 = 0.6 to find an approximate value for α
(c) Calculate, giving each answer to 4 decimal places,
(i) the value of x2
(ii) the value of α
(3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) B1: correct derivative f'(x) = 8x e^(4x^2-1), in any form. (ii) B1: correct derivative g'(x) = 8/x, in any form. (2 marks)
(b) M1: eliminates e by setting their f'(x) = their g'(x) (of the correct forms Axe^(4x^2-1) and B/x, A,B ≠ 0) and proceeds via e^(4x^2-1) = 2/x^2 (or equivalent) to obtain 4x^2 − 1 = ln(2/x^2) or equivalent, e.g. via x^2 e^(4x^2-1) = 1 => ln(x^2) + (4x^2-1) = 0. A1*: obtains the printed answer 4x^2 + 2 ln x − 1 = 0 with sufficient working shown (the 'e' must be eliminated before the given answer) and no errors, following correct derivatives from part (a). (2 marks)
(c)(i) M1: attempts to use the iterative formula with x1 = 0.6, i.e. x2 = sqrt((1 − 2 ln 0.6)/4); may be implied by awrt 0.71 provided no incorrect working is seen. A1: x2 = awrt 0.7109. (ii) B1: α = 0.6706 (exactly to 4dp, not just awrt 0.6706). (3 marks)
questions.notes: The square root in the iterative formula was not visible in the raw OCR text (it only showed '(1 - 2 ln xn)/4'); it was reconstructed from the equation in part (b) (x^2 = (1-2lnx)/4) and confirmed numerically against the mark scheme's stated value x2 = 0.7109, which only matches if a square root is taken.

questions.question_text:
Figure 2 shows a sketch of the straight line l. Line l passes through the points A and B. Relative to a fixed origin O
• the point A has position vector 2i – 3j + 5k
• the point B has position vector 5i + 6j + 8k
(a) Find vector AB
(1)
Given that a point P lies on l such that
|AP| = 2|BP|
(b) find the possible position vectors of P.
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: AB = 3i + 9j + 3k, correct vector (allow as i,j,k form or as a column vector, but not as a mismatched/coordinate form). (1 mark)
(b) General marking principle: M1 for a correct complete strategy to find at least one position for P (may be implied by at least 2 correct components); A1 for one correct position for P; dM1 for a correct complete strategy to find both positions for P; A1 for both correct positions and no others. Main method: OP = OA + 2AB = (2i−3j+5k) + 2(3i+9j+3k) = 8i+15j+11k (P beyond B), and OP = OA + (2/3)AB = (2i−3j+5k) + (2/3)(3i+9j+3k) = 4i+3j+7k (P between A and B), using |AP|=2|BP| to determine the two possible ratios in which P divides (or externally divides) AB. Both correct position vectors: 8i + 15j + 11k and 4i + 3j + 7k. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
(a) Prove that
1/(cosec θ - 1) + 1/(cosec θ + 1) ≡ 2 tan θ sec θ, θ ≠ 90n°, n ∈ ℤ
(3)
(b) Hence solve, for 0 < x < 90°, the equation
1/(cosec 2x - 1) + 1/(cosec 2x + 1) = cot 2x sec 2x
Give each answer, in degrees, to one decimal place.
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: adds the two fractions to obtain a correct single fraction (not fractions over fractions), in any form, e.g. [(cosecθ+1)+(cosecθ−1)] / [(cosecθ−1)(cosecθ+1)], which simplifies to 2cosecθ/(cosec^2θ−1). M1: uses a correct Pythagorean identity anywhere in the attempt, e.g. cosec^2θ − 1 = cot^2θ (or sin^2θ+cos^2θ=1 within an equivalent approach). A1*: correct work with all necessary steps shown, proceeding via sine and cosine, leading to the given result 2 tan θ sec θ with no notational or bracketing errors, e.g. 2cosecθ/cot^2θ = 2sinθ/(sinθcos^2θ) = 2/cos^2θ = 2tanθsecθ. (3 marks)
(b) B1: deduces the correct equation using the result from part (a): 2 tan 2x sec 2x = cot 2x sec 2x. M1: factors out or cancels sec 2x to obtain an equation of the form λ·tan 2x = μ·cot 2x, leading to an equation of the form tan^2 2x = λ (or equivalently sin^2 2x = 1/3 or cos^2 2x = 2/3), λ ≠ 0. M1: correct order of operations from tan^2 2x = λ (or sin^2 2x = λ or cos^2 2x = λ or cos 4x = k), leading to at least one value for x (e.g. square roots then inverse tan and divide by 2). A1: correct values, awrt 17.6 and awrt 72.4 (degree symbol not required; extra values in range or answers in radians score A0). (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
Figure 3 shows the path of a small ball. The ball travels in a vertical plane above horizontal ground. The ball is thrown from the point represented by A and caught at the point represented by B. The height, H metres, of the ball above the ground has been plotted against the horizontal distance, x metres, measured from the point where the ball was thrown. With respect to a fixed origin O, the point A has coordinates (0, 2) and the point B has coordinates (20, 0.8), as shown in Figure 3. The ball reaches its maximum height when x = 9. A quadratic function, linking H with x, is used to model the path of the ball.
(a) Find H in terms of x.
(4)
(b) Give one limitation of the model.
(1)
Chandra is standing directly under the path of the ball at a point 16 m horizontally from O. Chandra can catch the ball if the ball is less than 2.5 m above the ground.
(c) Use the model to determine if Chandra can catch the ball.
(2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: uses H = ax^2+bx+c to model the path, uses x=0, H=2 correctly placed to find c=2, and uses x=20, H=0.8 together with dH/dx=0 at x=9 (i.e. the vertex condition) to set up equations in a and b. dM1: forms 2 full equations in a and b from the constant term, the point (20, 0.8), and the maximum at x=9. ddM1: solves the 2 simultaneous equations in a and b (may be done by calculator, method not checked). A1: correct equation H = -0.03x^2 + 0.54x + 2. [Equivalent vertex-form method: H = A + B(x-9)^2, using both endpoints (0,2) and (20,0.8) to find A=4.43, B=-0.03, giving H = 4.43 - 0.03(x-9)^2 — an equally valid correct form, and note this alternative method uses no calculus at all.] (4 marks)
(b) B1: gives a suitable limitation focused on why the model may break down, e.g. 'the path is unlikely to be parabolic', 'air resistance has not been considered', 'wind may affect the path of the ball', 'the ball is not a particle so has dimensions/size'. Vague single-word answers (e.g. just 'friction' or 'spin') or statements about the model being invalid outside the range of the throw are not accepted. (1 mark)
(c) M1: substitutes x=16 into their quadratic model to obtain a value for H. A1: H = 2.96 (dependent on a correct equation), with correct conclusion that Chandra cannot catch the ball since 2.96 > 2.5. (2 marks)
questions.notes: This question is really about fitting a quadratic model to given data points plus a known vertex location (a curve-fitting/modelling question), which does not map cleanly onto any of the 16 fixed topics. 'differentiation' is used as the closest available tag because the main mark-scheme method sets dH/dx = 0 at x = 9 to locate the vertex, but an equally valid alternative method in the mark scheme (vertex form H = A + B(x-9)^2, using the two endpoints) uses no calculus at all. Flagging this as a possible gap in the topic vocabulary rather than silently forcing a tag.

questions.question_text:
Figure 4 shows a sketch of the curve C with parametric equations
x = (t+3)^2
y = 1 - t^3
-2 ≤ t ≤ 1
The point P with coordinates (4, 2) lies on C.
(a) Using parametric differentiation, show that the tangent to C at P has equation
3x + 4y = 20
(5)
The curve C is used to model the profile of a slide at a water park. Units are in metres, with y being the height of the slide above water level.
(b) Find, according to the model, the greatest height of the slide above water level.
(1)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: uses the given coordinates (4,2) to deduce the correct value t = -1 (if more than one value of t is offered and t=-1 is not clearly selected, this mark is not scored). M1: attempts dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) with the differentiated equations dx/dt = 2(t+3) and dy/dt = -3t^2 (both parameters must be differentiated, however poorly). M1: uses their numerical value of t (=-1, not 4) in their dy/dx expression to obtain a value, dy/dx = -3(-1)^2 / [2(-1+3)] = -3/4. ddM1: applies a correct straight-line method with their gradient -3/4, obtained from an attempt at parametric differentiation, with x=4 and y=2 correctly placed (depends on both previous M marks). A1*: correct equation 3x + 4y = 20 as printed, with no errors, and with at least one intermediate step shown. (5 marks)
(b) B1: maximum height is 9m (or equivalent, e.g. 9 metres) — occurs at the end of the given domain, t=-2, since y = 1 - t^3 is decreasing as t increases, so the greatest y is at the smallest t: y = 1 - (-2)^3 = 9. (1 mark)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
Figure 5 shows a sketch of part of the curve C with equation
y = 8x^2 e^(-3x), x ≥ 0
The finite region R, shown shaded in Figure 5, is bounded by
• the curve C
• the line with equation x = 1
• the x-axis
Find the exact area of R, giving your answer in the form
A + Be^(-3)
where A and B are rational numbers to be found.
(5)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: obtains the integral of 8x^2 e^(-3x) by integration by parts to reach the form [-(8/3)x^2 e^(-3x)] + ∫(16/3)x e^(-3x) dx (the '8' may be missing at this stage and still score). A1: correct expression, simplified or unsimplified. dM1: attempts integration by parts again on ∫(16/3)x e^(-3x) dx to obtain the form [Axe^(-3x)] - ∫B e^(-3x) dx, A,B ≠ 0 (may be seen in isolation; depends on the first method mark; the by-parts-twice 'DI method' is an accepted equivalent route). M1: substitutes the limits 1 and 0 into the full integrated expression -(8/3)x^2e^(-3x) - (16/9)xe^(-3x) - (16/27)e^(-3x) and subtracts the right way round, using e^0 = 1. A1: correct exact answer 16/27 - (136/27)e^(-3) (allow equivalent exact fractions; isw once the correct answer is seen). (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Express
1 / (V(25 - V))
in partial fractions.
(2)
The volume, V microlitres, of a plant cell t hours after the plant is watered is modelled by the differential equation
dV/dt = (1/10) V(25 - V)
The plant cell has an initial volume of 20 microlitres.
(b) Find, according to the model, the time taken, in minutes, for the volume of the plant cell to reach 24 microlitres.
(5)
(c) Show that
V = A / (e^(-kt) + B)
where A, B and k are constants to be found.
(3)
The model predicts that there is an upper limit, L microlitres, on the volume of the plant cell.
(d) Find the value of L, giving a reason for your answer.
(2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: sets 1/(V(25-V)) = P/V + Q/(25-V) and uses a correct method (e.g. 1 = P(25-V)+QV, substituting V=0 or V=25) to identify at least one constant. A1: correct partial fractions 1/(V(25-V)) = 1/(25V) + 1/(25(25-V)), in any equivalent form. (2 marks)
(b) M1: separates variables and recognises that ∫1/(V(25-V)) dV is required, reaching the form p ln V - q ln(25-V) (or equivalent) for the integration. A1ft: fully correct equation following through their P and Q, e.g. (1/25)ln V - (1/25)ln(25-V) = t/10 (+c) (the '+c' not required at this stage). M1: states or uses t=0, V=20 consistently to find the constant of integration. dM1: states or uses V=24 and proceeds to find a value for t (depends on the previous method mark and on an attempt to integrate both sides, however poor). A1: correct value t = 4/3 hours = awrt 43 minutes (or exact 24 ln 6 minutes) — units must be minutes. (5 marks)
(c) M1: uses fully correct log work, having obtained the constant of integration, to eliminate all the logs including from e.g. e^(ln4) (condone sign/coefficient slips only), e.g. ln[V/(4(25-V))] = 2.5t => V/(4(25-V)) = e^(2.5t). M1: proceeds from this equation using correct algebra to make V the subject, e.g. V = 4e^(2.5t)(25-V) => V + 4Ve^(2.5t) = 100e^(2.5t) => V = 100e^(2.5t)/(1+4e^(2.5t)), then divides numerator and denominator by e^(2.5t) to realise V = 100/(e^(-2.5t)+4). A1: correct expression (not just correct values for the constants): V = 100/(e^(-2.5t)+4), i.e. A=100, B=4, k=2.5. (3 marks)
(d) B1: correct value of 25 seen (allow e.g. '<25' or '≤25'; condoning '>25' means the following mark is not then available). B1: gives a valid reason depending on a correct final equation from (c), e.g. as t→∞, e^(-2.5t)→0, so V→100/4=25 [alternatively, using the differential equation directly: dV/dt=0 when V=25, or dV/dt<0 if V>25]. (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
The world human population, P billions, is modelled by the equation
P = ab^t
where a and b are constants and t is the number of years after 2004. Using the estimated population figures for the years from 2004 to 2007, a graph is plotted of log10 P against t. The points lie approximately on a straight line with
• gradient 0.0054
• intercept 0.81 on the log10 P axis
(a) Estimate, to 3 decimal places, the value of a and the value of b.
(4)
In the context of the model,
(b) (i) interpret the value of the constant a,
(ii) interpret the value of the constant b.
(2)
(c) Use the model to estimate the world human population in 2030
(2)
(d) Comment on the reliability of the answer to part (c).
(1)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) Taking log10 of P=ab^t gives log10 P = log10 a + t·log10 b, so log10 b = gradient = 0.0054 and log10 a = intercept = 0.81. M1: correct strategy to get a numerical expression/value for a or b, e.g. a = 10^0.81 or b = 10^0.0054 (may be implied by a = awrt 6.46 or b = awrt 1.01 if no incorrect work is seen). A1: correct value for a or b (allow 3sf here). M1: correct strategy to get numerical values for both a and b. A1: correct values a = 6.457 and b = 1.013, both to 3dp. (4 marks)
(b)(i) B1ft: correct interpretation of a, following through their value, referencing 'billions', e.g. 'the world population in billions in 2004' (i.e. at t=0). (ii) B1ft: correct interpretation of b, following through their value, referencing 'each year'/'yearly', e.g. 'b = 1.013 represents the scale factor of the yearly increase in the world population', or 'the population rises by 1.3% each year'. (2 marks)
(c) M1: substitutes t=26 into their model P=ab^t to find a value for P (2030 is 26 years after 2004). A1: correct value, awrt 9 billion (units required; just 'awrt 9' without units is A0). (2 marks)
(d) B1: states the answer is unreliable, with reference to the fact that the data used for the model (2004-2007) is a long way in time from 2030, e.g. 'not reliable since the data used for the model covered 2004-2007 and it would not be sensible to assume the model still holds in 2030'. (1 mark)

questions.question_text:
The circle C1 has equation
x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 14y + 33 = 0
(a) Find
(i) the coordinates of the centre of C1
(ii) the radius of C1
(3)
A different circle C2
• has centre with coordinates (-6, -8)
• has radius k, where k is a constant
Given that C1 and C2 intersect at 2 distinct points,
(b) find the range of values of k, writing your answer in set notation.
(5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) B1: centre (3, -7), obtained by completing the square: (x-3)^2 + (y+7)^2 = 9 + 49 - 33. (ii) M1: uses a correct strategy to find the radius or radius^2, i.e. (x-3)^2 + (y+7)^2 = 25. A1: radius = 5 (do not allow ±5 or 25 as the final answer). (3 marks)
(b) M1: uses Pythagoras correctly on the centre found in (a) and the given centre (-6,-8) of C2 to find the distance between centres: sqrt((3-(-6))^2 + (-7-(-8))^2) = sqrt(82). A1ft: correct distance sqrt(82) (follow through their centre from (a); allow decimals to 3sf, awrt 9.06). dM1: correct strategy for one of the limits, e.g. adds or subtracts their radius 5 to/from the distance between centres sqrt(82) (since for two circles with one fixed centre and a variable radius k to intersect at 2 distinct points, k must lie strictly between |distance-radius| and distance+radius). A1: correct limits sqrt(82)-5 and sqrt(82)+5 (allow decimals to 3sf, awrt 4.06 and awrt 14.1). A1: correct answer using exact values in set notation, {k : sqrt(82)-5 < k < sqrt(82)+5} (equivalent set notation forms accepted, e.g. using '|' for ':', or interval notation (sqrt(82)-5, sqrt(82)+5); plain inequality notation without set notation is not accepted for this final mark). (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
The curve C has equation
(x + y)^3 = 3x^2 - 3y - 2
(a) Find an expression for dy/dx in terms of x and y.
(5)
The point P(1, 0) lies on C.
(b) Show that the normal to C at P has equation
y = -2x + 2
(2)
(c) Prove that the normal to C at P does not meet C again. You should use algebra for your proof and make your reasoning clear.
(5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: differentiates implicitly, applying the chain rule to (x+y)^3 to obtain a term of the form k(x+y)^2(1 + dy/dx), k a non-zero constant (condone missing brackets if intention is clear). A1: correct term 3(x+y)^2(1 + dy/dx). A1: correct differentiation of the other side, 6x - 3(dy/dx). M1: valid attempt to make dy/dx the subject with exactly 2 distinct terms in dy/dx — one coming from differentiating (x+y)^3 and the other from differentiating '-3y' (look for (...±...)dy/dx = ... => dy/dx = ...). A1: fully correct expression dy/dx = [6x - 3(x+y)^2] / [3(x+y)^2 + 3], or any equivalent correct form, e.g. [2x-(x+y)^2] / [(x+y)^2+1]. (5 marks)
(b) M1: substitutes x=1, y=0 into their dy/dx from part (a) to obtain the tangent gradient (=1/2), takes the negative reciprocal to get the normal gradient (=-2), and applies a correct straight-line method with x=1, y=0 correctly placed. A1*: correct equation y = -2x + 2 as printed, with no errors, following a correct dy/dx from part (a). (2 marks)
(c) M1: substitutes y = -2x+2 into the equation of C (or equivalently x=(2-y)/2) to obtain an equation in a single variable (not necessarily a cubic yet). A1: correct cubic equation with terms collected and '=0' seen, e.g. x^3 - 3x^2 + 18x - 16 = 0 (or in y: y^3 + 60y = 0). dM1: uses the fact that (x-1), or y, is a known factor (since (x,y)=(1,0) is the known intersection point) to establish the quadratic factor, e.g. by inspection or long division, to obtain 3 terms. ddM1: with a correct cubic equation and the correct quadratic factor (or a multiple of it, e.g. x^2-2x+16 or y^2+60), attempts to show the quadratic factor has no real roots, e.g. via the discriminant, completing the square, calculus, or direct solution. A1: fully correct concluding argument requiring correct work, a justification depending on the strategy used, and a conclusion, e.g. discriminant of x^2-2x+16=0 is (-2)^2 - 4(1)(16) = 4 - 64 < 0, so no real roots, so the normal and curve only meet once (at P) and the normal does not meet C again. (5 marks)
